  • Industry observers note that if you live in an area that’s prone to power outages and you want to keep the lights on and prevent food in your fridge from spoiling, having a generator is essential.
  • Sources indicate that A portable generator is a gas-powered machine that you can carry or wheel over short distances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Industry observers note that if you live in an area that’s prone to power outages and you want to keep the lights on and prevent food in your fridge from spoiling, having a generator is essential. There are types of generators that are affordable, versatile, and portable; others types are whole-home standby options that conveniently turn on automatically and produce enough energy to power an entire home. Determining which type is best for your home depends on your budget, what you’re willing to go without when a power outage strikes, and where you live.

Sources indicate that A portable generator is a gas-powered machine that you can carry or wheel over short distances. It functions as a temporary power source when the grid goes down, producing enough juice to keep the essentials running, including a fridge, lights and electronics. Portable generators have outlets, so you can power many of your appliances.

“A portable generator can be a good solution for homeowners who only need to power a few essential items for short periods of time and don’t mind manually setting up the generator, storing fuel, and connecting extension cords,” indicates Amy Northway, president of Power Solutions Specialist, a Briggs & Stratton backup generator dealer in Houston.

In a recent development, honda’s 2200-watt inverter generator is super quiet and can power a refrigerator for about 4 hours on half a tank of gas. Read the review.

Sources indicate that A standby generator is permanently installed outside your home that produces enough electricity to power an entire house indefinitely in the event of a power outage. These machines connect directly to your home’s electrical panel and use your natural gas line for fuel. A standby generator automatically turns on in seconds when the power goes out, seamlessly transferring your power source from the grid to the generator.

“Homeowners who rely on air conditioning during Houston’s summer heat, work from home, have medical equipment, travel frequently, or simply want their home to operate normally during an outage often find that a standby generator provides far greater value and peace of mind,” states Northway.

Choosing the best home generator comes down to budget, power demands, and how often you face power outages in your region.

A portable generator is significantly cheaper than a whole home standby generator. You’ll pay about $500 to $3,000 for a portable generator, depending on its power output. In comparison, it costs around $8,000 to $16,000 or more for an installed standby generator depending on the amount of electrical upgrades or gas line work that needs to be done on the house to accommodate the generator.

While standby generators do have a higher upfront cost, you can recoup most if not all of that when you sell your home. The return on investment (ROI) of a standby generator is around 95 percent, according to Zonda/JLC, a data and analytics company for the home building industry, and can exceed 100 percent in regions prone to extreme weather.

Most homes can operate normally during a power outage with a generator that produces around 20,000 watts. A whole home standby generator can produce enough wattage to cover that amount. In comparison, a portable power station only produces 7,500 to 10,000 watts, enough to power essentials, including a fridge, lights, television, microwave, and small appliances. Most portable generators don’t produce enough power to keep electric-powered HVAC systems online.

Sources indicate that the stability of the grid in your area is also a factor. If you live in an area in which power outages are common and can last days, it may make sense to invest in a whole home standby generator that doesn’t require set-up and can keep your home running as normal when an outage strikes. “During a hurricane or major storm, fuel can be difficult to find, temperatures can become dangerous, and outages may last for days,” Northway says. “A standby generator connected to natural gas or propane can continue operating without requiring the homeowner to refuel or even be home when the outage occurs.”.

A standby generator kicks on automatically when a power outage strikes and doesn’t require setup or running extension cords, making it more convenient to use. That stated, portable models are more versatile. You can use them at home or take them on the road to power an RV during a camping trip or power tools at a jobsite. “A portable generator can be a good solution for homeowners who only need to power a few essential items for short periods of time and don’t mind manually setting up the generator, storing fuel, and connecting extension cords,” Northway states.

Choosing between a portable or standby generator comes down to budget, energy demands, and whether you live in an area in which extreme weather is common, says Northway. “If the goal is occasional backup power for a few items, a portable generator may be sufficient,” she says. “If the goal is comfort, convenience, and peace of mind during extended outages, a standby generator is typically the better long-term investment.”.

Industry observers note that power outages are a common problem during thunderstorms, so it’s a good idea to have a backup strategy ready to go when the lights go out. Gas and propane generators are common choices for home backup power, RV use, and camping trips.

Recent findings suggest that propane generators, for example, burn cleaner than gasoline generators, but tend to be more costly to purchase and operate. Gasoline generators are more efficient, but the fuel has a shorter shelf life and may not always be available in emergencies due to panic buying at local gas stations. This guide outlines other differences between the two that will help you decide which type of generator is right for your home.

Having a basic understanding of how the different types of generators work can help decide on the right choice for your home. A propane generator operates by burning the propane in an internal combustion engine. This process creates mechanical energy, which is used to turn a rotor within a magnetic field to generate electricity that can then be used to power appliances and other electronic devices.

It has been revealed that choosing a propane emergency generator for the home makes it easier to stockpile fuel for emergencies. Ken Goodrich, Founder and CEO of Kenerator, says “Propane is a great option for home backup power because it stores well and burns clean. Even when natural gas is temporarily shut off due to a natural disaster or infrastructure damage, a propane tank will continue to supply power.” Additionally, propane burns cleaner than gasoline, so you can expect the best propane generators to require less maintenance and produce fewer emissions.

Understanding how much propane a generator uses is key to deciding on the right model for your home, since propane generators tend to have lower fuel efficiency than gasoline generators. “Additionally, propane suppliers usually deliver to customers on a routine basis, so the homeowner needs to ensure they have enough propane to make it through an average outage,” notes Goodrich. It should also be mentioned that propane generators typically cost more up front and have higher operating costs, so they may not be the best choice for those looking for a cheap solution.

Industry observers note that whether you are looking to purchase a gas or propane generator, it’s good to know how the appliance operates. Generally, the operation of a gasoline generator can be described as a process that converts chemical energy into mechanical energy, which in turn produces electrical energy. More specifically, the engine burns gasoline to spin a shaft, which rotates magnets or electromagnetic fields near the stator, a stationary coil of wires. This induces a change in the magnetic field, creating an electrical current in the coils, that can then be used to power connected appliances and electrical devices.

The main benefit of a gas generator is that these appliances are more affordable to purchase and operate than propane generators, though there can be some fluctuation in the energy efficiency between specific models, so don’t hesitate to ask how much gas does a generator use when researching potential products.

Goodrich mentions that “portable gasoline generators are good options for camping and construction sites,” so you can make use of your generator even when you aren’t at home. Goodrich goes on to say that “gasoline generators are affordable, portable, easy to find, and simple to use,” making them a great choice for just about any home.

In a recent development, while gasoline generators may be cheaper to purchase and operate, gas does not burn as cleanly as propane, so there is a higher risk that these appliances will break down or require frequent maintenance to keep them in good condition. “Gasoline engines use carburetors, as opposed to mixers, which clog easily if not run on a weekly or monthly schedule,” Goodrich points out.

If you like the potential of both propane and gasoline generators, but can’t decide between one or the other, then you may find the best dual-fuel generators to be a good alternative. These generators work by switching between gasoline and propane using a manual or automatic fuel selector.

Sources indicate that while the engine has the same combustion cycle for both fuels, it utilizes a built-in carburetor to atomize gasoline for combustion, but when using propane, the fuel passes through a separate external line and regulator before it is pulled into the engine by the vacuum created by the piston. Goodrich says that dual-fuel generators are “definitely a viable option. A lot of homeowners like having propane for its clean burn and long storage life, with gasoline as a backup if they run through their propane supply.”.

Sources indicate that westinghouse iGen4500 has a 3.4-gal. gas tank that can run quietly for up to 18 hours; has a variety of ports but weighs 100+ lbs. Read the review.

In a recent development, propane generators use safer, easier to store, and cleaner-burning fuel than gasoline generators; gas generators are more affordable to purchase and operate, with better fuel efficiency. “For most homeowners looking for reliable backup power, propane is the better long-term solution. That remarked, if you’re looking for something more budget-friendly, gasoline can still get the job done,” claims Goodrich.

After gaining a basic understanding of the pros and cons between propane vs. gasoline generators, it’s a good idea to start your search by reading up on the best generator brands, then researching individual products that offer the features you want. Keep in mind that at the end of the day, a dual-fuel generator, powered by propane and natural gas, will offer you the best of both worlds so you are prepared for any emergency.

In a recent development, power outages can be difficult to weather any time of year, but not having a working heater when temperatures are frigid can be hard on you and your home. When there’s a winter storm in the forecast, there’s no time to lose. If you start preparing for inclement weather now, even before there’s a whisper about bad weather, and you’ll be in better shape should blizzards, nor’easters, or bomb cyclones head your way.

Sources indicate that make sure you have a good supply of batteries (and if they’re rechargeable batteries, ensure that they’re fully charged!) in a range of sizes for all your emergency needs. Have spares ready for flashlights and radios as well as for smoke detectors, clocks, and other necessities that can run on battery backup.

How many times have you clicked on several flashlights in your junk drawer before finding one that actually works? Carefully test each of your flashlights and figure out which ones work and which don’t. Refresh the batteries and test them again, ditching the flashlights that still don’t work. Purchase additional flashlights if you need them (can you really have too many?). Make sure there’s a “good” light for each member of the family, at the very least. Don’t plan on using candles; flashlights are safer.

Sources indicate that always top off your cars’ fuel tanks when you’re expecting a big storm. Gas station pumps run on electricity and if the power goes out, you won’t be able to get gasoline. If you have a gas-powered portable generator, fill some gas cans, too, so you can keep the generator going.

It has been revealed that A key component of a winter survival kit is a means of charging your mobile phone in your car, whether that’s a car charger for your phone or the right cord to connect auto to phone. With a full gas tank and a car charger, you’ll be able to keep your phone working even if you lose power for an extended period of time. You may also want to invest in a solar phone charger, which would allow you to charge your phone without sitting in your driveway.

Sources indicate that if you have landline telephone service, it’s worth keeping an old corded landline phone around. Modern phones that plug into wall outlets will not work during a power outage, and having access to a usable landline will help you conserve your cell phone battery.

Industry observers note that if the power goes out during winter, how will you keep warm? Devise a proposal now, before you’re in that situation. Even a gas-powered furnace requires electricity to run the fan that sends warm air through the vents. If you have a gas fireplace, consider installing a battery backup for the starter if you don’t already have one. If you rely on a wood stove for heat, stock up on firewood. Do not use a propane heater inside the home unless it is one specifically designed for indoor use; carbon monoxide can build up and create a deadly hazard.

Recent findings suggest that mr. Heater’s Portable Buddy Heater quickly heats up to 225 sq. ft. of space and has a tip-over safety mechanism. Read the review.

According to recent reports, when a heavy storm is in the forecast, stock up on drinking water, and fill up the bathtub and washing machine so you’ll have enough water for washing and for flushing the toilets. The PennState extension service states Americans use 50 to 100 gallons of water per person per day, but that kind of stockpile may be hard to achieve in an emergency situation. You will want to have on hand at least a gallon of potable water per person per day.

According to recent reports, if your home relies on municipal water, your water taps will keep flowing in the event of a power outage. But homes on well water aren’t so lucky—well pumps won’t work without electricity.

According to recent reports, how will you cook if you lose electricity? If you have gas appliances, you should be able to light the pilot light with a match if you lose power. But if you have an electric stovetop and oven, you won’t be able to use your stove. You can, however, use a propane grill or an open fire to cook outdoors. If that’s your blueprint, refill the propane tank, or buy a cord of wood. And whatever your appliance situation, make sure you have a manual can opener.

Lowering the temperature of your refrigerator and freezer before the storm hits will help them stay cooler longer if the power goes out, thus increasing the likelihood that your food will be safe to eat after the power outage. Consider moving perishables like milk and meat into the freezer so they’ll stay colder. To conserve the cold air inside, avoid opening the refrigerator doors more than you absolutely have to.

If a winter power outage lasts more than a few days, you may run out of fresh food (or a means to prepare food). For this reason, it’s a good idea to keep plenty of nonperishable foods with long shelf lives like nut butters, canned fruit and juices, granola bars, and crackers on hand to keep yourself nourished.

Radios may seem a relic of the past, but these old-fashioned devices may just save your bacon if you lose power for an extended period. When modern methods of emergency alerts such as TVs and phones are offline, an emergency radio with fresh batteries may be your lifeline to news and information about dangerous conditions, even evacuation alerts. Better yet, select a radio can be charged in multiple ways. The Eton Odyssey radio, for example, can be charged via hand crank, USB-C, solar, and rechargeable and alkaline battery.

The Midland WR120B can be programmed to check weather in 25 local regions, so you can stay on top of loved ones’ forecasts Read the review.

Industry observers note that loss of power could be an excuse for a fun “campout” in the living room. Ahead of the storm, make sure your tent and sleeping bags are in good shape, or acquire these items if you don’t have them. Ensure you have plenty of heavy blankets, too. Then, when the power is out and temps in the house drop, set up the tent and unroll the sleeping bags. Body heat from people together in an enclosed space will help keep everyone warm. And you’ll have a fun story to tell!

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve been meaning to caulk your windows, do it before cold weather strikes. Check the weatherstripping around your doors; odds are it’s seen better days. If your budget allows, replace or supplement your attic insulation. A less expensive way of sealing out some cold is to purchase some door draft stoppers, which you can tuck away in a closet until they are needed.

According to recent reports, the worst time to buy a generator is the day you need one. If you live in an area that frequently loses power, consider purchasing a portable power station or a backup generator, which can be switched on manually or can automatically kick in when the power goes out. You can get generators powered by gasoline, natural gas, propane, or diesel (or even dual-fuel or inverter generators); solar generators are also an option but of course require a solar setup too.

Dual-fuel generators offer the flexibility to run on either gasoline or propane, making them a versatile option for backup power. But with so many available, and many costing over $1,000, we tested a range of top models to help you find the right fit. Bottom line: Dual-fuel generators offer flexibility and power for home and outdoor use. Our tests highlight the best models to suit various needs and budgets.

Multifuel generators use gasoline or propane to provide electric power to your home, campground, or jobsite. But before buying a dual-fuel generator, consider whether it will meet your needs.

One key aspect of dual-fuel generators is you cannot run them indoors since they produce toxic fumes. Instead, you must set them up outside in a sheltered location and provide electrical power to appliances through an extension cord.

They are relatively heavy, weighing 100 to 200 pounds on average, and typically loud, sometimes exceeding the acceptable volumes allowed at RV parks. An inverter generator may be a better choice if you want a quiet generator. These generators have an enclosed body and supply power using a computer-controlled inverter instead of a noisier alternator.

However, if you need a decent amount of power, can see yourself regularly using more than one fuel type, and can handle a little extra weight and noise, a dual-fuel generator may be right for you.

It has been revealed that we awarded points to each model using a rubric considering ease of use, noise, portability, power, and value. The better a generator performed a test, the more points it received. After testing, we averaged the points to determine top performers.

To find the best dual-fuel generator for your home, campground, or worksite, consider the factors listed below, including fuel efficiency, fuel tank capacity, power output, and control panel configuration.

Industry observers note that dual-fuel generators have an isolated gasoline tank with a fuel capacity that ranges from as small as 2 gallons to more than 10 gallons. The larger the fuel tank on the generator, the longer the generator can provide gasoline-based power. But, as tank size increases, so does the size of the generator.

Fuel capacity does not affect how much propane you can use with your dual-fuel generator. Propane gas is stored under pressure in canisters, which attach to the generator with a hose and pressure regulator for direct fuel consumption.

Industry observers note that the power output on dual-fuel generators is measured in watts. Manufacturers’ specs include peak power output and running power output. Peak power output refers to the maximum number of watts the generator can provide at any one time. Running power output equals the average number of watts produced during use.

Dual-fuel generators generally produce a power output from 1,000 watts to over 12,000 watts, depending on their size. Gasoline produces a higher wattage than propane, so many manufacturers of dual-fuel technology break wattage into propane peak and running outputs and gasoline peak and running outputs.

For greater power output needs, consumers may need to consider a standby generator rather than a portable dual-fuel option.

You can start your dual-fuel generator with an electric start switch or a recoil cord.

A generator’s operating noise level is measured in decibels. To understand the range of sound produced by a generator, consider these common sounds and their equivalent operating dB level:.

Many dual-fuel generators produce 50 to 90 dB of noise, depending on fuel type (gasoline runs louder than propane) and power output. The most common range is between 65 dB and 75 dB, comparable to the sound of normal conversation.

The quietest dual-fuel generators combine dual-fuel technology and inverter technology to create a dual-fuel inverter generator.

Dual-fuel generators are typically large and heavy, with hoses or tanks that make them difficult to carry and move. Thus, some manufacturers include wheel kits for tilting the generator back and rolling it to the desired location.

Industry observers note that you may also be able to purchase a wheel kit separately to add to your existing generator or replace an older wheel kit that doesn’t work well anymore. Either way, a wheel kit makes transporting a portable dual-fuel generator much easier.

It has been revealed that lift hook bars are handy on jobsites, allowing workers to attach the generator to a hook-and-pulley system and raise or lower it instead of carrying it up or down stairs or ladders. In industrial settings, this feature helps raise the generator onto a walkway or platform.

A lift hook bar will increase the generator’s weight (and likely the price), so don’t look for a generator with this feature unless you truly proposal to use it.

Recent findings suggest that most dual-fuel generators are between 22 inches long by 22 inches wide by 22 inches high and 35 inches long by 30 inches wide by 30 inches high. They typically weigh between 100 and 250 pounds.

It has been revealed that if you plan to move the generator frequently, figure size and weight prominently into your decision. Make sure the model you choose fits into your vehicle so you can transport it as needed. Remember, however, that larger, heavier motors are also the most powerful. You’ll want to find the right balance of size, weight, and power to meet your needs.

Gasoline and propane each have their pros and cons as fuel options. Gasoline is easier to find, but propane costs less. Propane is a better fuel source in hot summer weather, while gas burns better in the cold. A dual-fuel generator lets you choose one or the other based on immediate circumstances.

In a recent development, using both fuel sources, one after the other, greatly increases a generator’s runtime. Users can run to the gas station to refuel while the generator keeps providing power on propane.

Dual-fuel generators let users:.

Before buying a dual-fuel generator, consider the answers to the following frequently asked questions.

A dual-fuel generator operates like a single-fuel generator, except it can burn propane and gasoline to produce electrical energy. It converts mechanical energy produced by the burning fuels to force the movement of electrical charges and generate electricity.

Recent findings suggest that while some single-fuel generators can be adapted for use with natural gas, this isn’t the case with dual-fuel generators. Unless specially designed, dual-fuel generators do not run on natural gas and cannot be adapted for this purpose.

Recent findings suggest that propane gas is less expensive than gasoline, nearly impossible to spill, and burns cleaner, resulting in less wear on the engine over time. Running a dual-fuel generator on propane will save money but slightly decrease the machine’s peak and running watts.

Runtime is determined by fuel efficiency and fuel tank capacity. On average, a standard dual-fuel generator runs about 8 to 10 hours on propane.

If power is the goal, then the DuroMax dual-fuel generator is one of the best options to help ensure the campsite or essential home appliances have power for hours.

Depending on how much wattage a home draws under normal situations, attaching a high-capacity dual-fuel generator to its electrical system may be possible, but it’s not a DIY project.An electrician must install a transfer switch connecting the generator to the home’s electrical main. When the power goes out, the transfer switch automatically switches the incoming power from the grid to the generator. In most cases, the generator will be classified as a “standby generator” because it’s always ready to start generating electricity. Most portable generators are too small to run an entire home.

Generators running on gasoline are typically louder than those running on propane since burning propane requires less energy.

As with most outdoor tools and large household appliances, you will want to take dual-fuel generators to a local recycling plant for recycling.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The order was issued by a Mississippi state court Oct. 12; the case has just been removed to federal court, which will now consider the defendant's arguments against the injunction. Here's the key passage from the injunction, a temporary restraining order that was issued before the defendant could respond:.

Here's the heart of plaintiffs' argument:.

Defendants argue that the order isn't authorized by the Mississippi's Protection from Domestic Abuse Law or by the Mississippi rules governing ordinary temporary restraining orders. But it also argues (I think correctly) that is an overbroad prior restraint that violates the First Amendment:.

The order does not merely prohibit threats or harassment. It prohibits speech about the Plaintiffs, their families, and their lawyers—whether truthful or false, threatening or harmless, harassing or not. And it does so before that speech occurs. The Supreme Court has repeatedly condemned such prior restraints, particularly when imposed without notice or an opportunity to be heard.

According to recent reports, the Court need not decide whether Mr. Hughes's commentary was fair, tasteful, or justified. The question is whether the law permits this order. It does not. The order should be dissolved, and the motion for a preliminary injunction denied….

In a recent development, A judicial order "forbidding certain communications when issued in advance of the time that such communications are to occur" is a prior restraint…. "Any system of prior restraints on communication bears a heavy presumption against its constitutional validity." Such restraints are unconstitutional "except in exceptional circumstances." .As the Supreme Court held in Organization for a Better Austin v. Keefe (1971), {the party seeking to suppress speech} "carries a heavy burden of showing justification for the imposition of such a restraint." ….

Industry observers note that the remedy for false or injurious statements lies in "actions under libel laws providing for redress and punishment, and not in proceedings to restrain the publication." [But t]he October 12 Order … does not impose consequences for particular statements adjudicated unlawful. It prohibits Mr. Hughes from speaking about entire categories of people in the future. That is a prior restraint in its most direct form which is presumed unconstitutional….

According to recent reports, test Masters Educ. Servs., Inc. v. Singh (5th Cir. 2005) … recognized that a court may enjoin "harassing communication" and "repeated invasions of privacy." But an injunction prohibiting all communication, rather than limiting itself to "threatening or harassing conduct," "swept too broadly" and constituted an unconstitutional restraint. Id.….

In a recent development, plaintiffs cannot justify the restraint merely by characterizing Mr. Hughes's commentary as malicious, coercive, or injurious. The Supreme Court rejected that reasoning in Keefe. There, the Court held that an individual's "interest in being free from public criticism of his business practices" did not justify an injunction against speech…. Plaintiffs may have remedies for unlawful conduct. But those remedies do not include an order forbidding Mr. Hughes from speaking about them at all….

Defendant also argues (again correctly, I think) that the order was unconstitutional because defendant wasn't given an opportunity to be heard before the order was entered:.

Recent findings suggest that the absence of notice presents a separate constitutional defect. In Carroll v. President & Commissioners of Princess Anne (1968), the Supreme Court set aside a short ex parte order restraining expression because of "a basic infirmity in the procedure by which it was obtained." The order "was issued ex parte, without notice to petitioners and without any effort, however informal, to invite or permit their participation in the proceedings.".

There is a place in our jurisprudence for ex parte issuance, without notice, of temporary restraining orders of short duration; There is no place within the area of basic freedoms guaranteed by the First Amendment for such orders where no showing is made that it is impossible to serve or to notify the opposing parties and to give them an opportunity to participate.

Industry observers note that the Court also rejected the suggestion that a later hearing could cure the problem. The availability of a subsequent opportunity to be heard "does not overcome the infirmity in the absence of a showing of justification for the ex parte nature of the proceedings.".

Sources indicate that the reason is straightforward. "The value of judicial decision-making … is substantially diluted where the process is ex parte, because the Court does not have available the fundamental instrument for judicial judgment: "an adversary proceeding in which both parties may participate." And where First Amendment freedoms are at stake, any order must be "couched in the narrowest terms that will accomplish the pin-pointed objective.".

The October 12 Order fails both principles. It was entered without notice or an adversary hearing. It contains no finding that notifying Mr. Hughes was impossible. And far from identifying a narrow category of unlawful speech, it prohibits virtually any online commentary concerning the Plaintiffs, their families, or their counsel.

Carroll is directly controlling on the constitutional defect. An ex parte order restraining expression cannot stand without a showing that notice and participation were impossible. No such showing appears here….

Electricity and solar are the main power sources for outdoor Christmas lights, though you can also sometimes find battery-operated Christmas lights. Of the two, electricity is by far the more reliable. Electricity provides consistent power, though it also requires extension cords and access to an outdoor outlet in the right location.

In a recent development, solar-powered Christmas lights are less common but are still a viable option. They’re an energy saver, generating energy via a solar panel during the day, but they aren’t without their flaws. The biggest problem is power consistency. Solar power must be stored to keep the lights running after the sun goes down. Many of these lights shine brightly for about 1 or 2 hours but then dim as power fades. Yes, they save power, but they’re not nearly as bright or consistent as electric lights.

Sources indicate that LED Christmas light bulbs use light-emitting diodes instead of filaments like incandescent bulbs. The diodes require less energy and last longer than filaments, creating a long-lasting, energy-efficient light bulb. LED lights also remain cool to the touch, reducing the risk of fire. Outdoor LED Christmas lights come in a wider variety of colors than incandescent ones. When paired with smart features, they can create a rainbow of options.

When hanging outdoor Christmas lights, recruit a helper, get a sturdy ladder, and prepare for at least a few hours of work. Start with a string near an electrical outlet and hang your Christmas lights by following the roofline. Have your helper hold the ladder for stability. If the lights you’re hanging don’t have clips, you can attach them with nails, a staple gun, or removable light clips. Of these options, the removable clips are easiest and cause the least damage to the home.

In a recent development, unlike indoor Christmas lights, outdoor Christmas lights should be 100 percent waterproof. If they’re not, they could short out the first time it rains or snows. Check the IP rating, which consists of two digits. The first number indicates dust and debris resistance, and the second indicates water resistance on a scale of 0 to 9. Waterproof outdoor Christmas lights should have a rating of at least 4 (in the second digit) or higher. Lights with a 4 or 5 can resist light rain, though they may not do well in extremely wet weather.

According to recent reports, yes, Christmas outdoor lights are safe to leave on all night. However, you might want to connect them to a timer to save energy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This short upcoming article of mine has now been published in the Notre Dame Law Review. The Introduction:.

Industry observers note that there are many important significant-picture questions about original meaning and the Free Speech, Free Press, Assembly, and Petition Clauses. This short Essay will leave those questions for others. Instead, it will offer as illustrations some specific, concrete questions—and, in some instances, answers—about original meaning and the freedom of expression. I hope these narrow illustrations can help us think about the broader questions.

From the table of contents, which should illustrate the subjects I cover:.

Industry observers note that I. Broad Evidence, and Silently Consistent Precedents A. "The Liberty of the Press Is Not Confined to Newspapers and Periodicals" B. Symbolic Expression C. Civil Liability II. Scant Evidence: Provoking a Riot III. Ambiguous Evidence: Enjoining Repetition of Libels.

Whether courts should shift the constitutional law of free expression to a more originalist footing is an important and difficult question. Perhaps it's a question that should be resolved entirely as a matter of constitutional theory—maybe such an approach is required by proper interpretive principles, or maybe it's forbidden by other principles (for instance, having to do with precedent).

But it's also possible that the answer may rest in part on how practically usable an originalist framework is likely to be. And to consider that, it's helpful to have in mind some practical questions. Some are already familiar, for instance questions related to damages liability in libel cases, obscenity law, and the like. This short Essay has aimed to help supplement those familiar examples with some others that haven't been much discussed; I hope others who think about the topic can find them useful.

I expect I'll post excerpts from the article in the coming days.

Industry observers note that as a gas, ammonia, hydrogen and nitrogen chemical compound is pungent and dangerous. But in its diluted household form, the nitrogen-based super cleaner is a workhorse in the war on common household dirt and grime. Ammonia is readily available, inexpensive, and potent, so a little goes a long way.

It has been revealed that before you buy ammonia, know that there are various types of household ammonia to choose from. You may see “cloudy” or “sudsy” versions—that’s ammonia with soap added, which is generally used for such domestic cleaning chores as treating stained clothing or scrubbing stovetops. We recommend opting for “clear” ammonia, which is suited to a wider variety of tasks (and you can always add a tablespoon or two of dish soap to make clear ammonia sudsy). You’ll also find ammonia that’s scented with lemon or pine to temper its stinging odor.

Sources indicate that the harsh smell serves as a warning, though: Working with ammonia absolutely requires caution. Pure chemical ammonia can cause severe burns and respiratory complications if it comes into contact with skin or is ingested. Even diluted in water, as is recommended for most cleaning purposes, ammonia can still be harmful.

Mixing ammonia and chlorine bleach creates a toxic gas called chloramine. Take great care not to combine them—doing so could have dire consequences.

According to recent reports, the most notable safety rule to remember is: Never mix ammonia with chlorine bleach. The result is a highly toxic chlorine gas that can produce headaches, seizures, and other symptoms. It’s crucial to keep this in mind if you’re using ammonia with laundry or to clean surfaces. You want to make absolutely sure not to mix it with a detergent or household cleaner that contains bleach.

According to recent reports, when using ammonia, be sure to wear chemical-resistant gloves and ventilate the area well. Be sure, too, to store it where pets and children can’t access it. Bearing these safety guidelines in mind, put ammonia to work around the home, as generations have done before us.

To achieve streak-free mirrors, windows, and crystal, mix 1 tablespoon clear ammonia with 2 cups water in a spray bottle. Spritz the solution onto glass items and wipe immediately with a soft, lint-free cloth for windows and crystal; paper towels work fine for mirrors.

According to recent reports, to remove stains on a concrete driveway, garage floor, or patio, mix 1 cup ammonia with 1 gallon of water in a bucket and apply it to the stain with a mop or large sponge. Let sit for about 20 minutes, and then scrub the stain with a bristled brush. Rinse the surface with clean water. If the stain isn’t completely gone after the area dries, repeat the process until you’re satisfied with the results.

In a recent development, if gold, silver, diamond, or platinum jewelry has lost its shine, mix 6 parts warm water to 1 part ammonia in a bowl (one that you don’t eat or cook with and add your jewelry. (Never use ammonia to clean pearls or other gems.) After 15 minutes, remove the jewelry with your gloved hand, and then gently scrape away any stubborn grime with a soft-bristled toothbrush (one that’s no longer in use or designated for cleaning). Allow it to soak for another 15 minutes, remove from the solution, and immediately rinse with warm water. Dispose of used ammonia solution down the drain while running the hot water. Polish the jewelry with a soft, lint-free cloth and let it dry.

In a recent development, stubborn stains on cotton, polyester, or nylon fabrics are no match for a solution of ⅔ cup clear ammonia, ⅔ cup dish soap, 6 tablespoons of baking soda, and 2 cups warm water. Mix in a bowl or bucket and apply generously to stains with a sponge or spray bottle. Let the treatment sit for about 30 minutes, then launder as usual. For tougher stains like blood or grass, treat the stain again with a solution of 1 part ammonia and 1 part warm water.

Recent findings suggest that note: Do not use ammonia on wool or silk, which can eat through the delicate fabrics. And remember never to mix ammonia with any laundry products that contain bleach.

Industry observers note that tackle caked-on grease on stove burners with this trick. Place each burner in a separate sealable plastic bag filled with ¼ cup ammonia. Seal each bag to keep fumes at bay, and place in a sink or washtub for 8 to 12 hours. Open the bags in a ventilated area, and remove all grease and dirt easily with a quick scrub of dish soap and water. Once the gunk is gone, thoroughly rinse the burners with water to get rid of ammonia residue. Let dry completely before using.

Mix one part clear ammonia and one part hot water in a sprayer or other bottle. Apply generously to the stain by spritzing or with a sponge. After about 10 minutes of dwell time, place a clean old towel over the stain and press with an iron, blasting with steam, for about 20 seconds. Check your progress: The stain should start transferring to the towel. Repeat, with steam ironing and more ammonia solution if needed, until the stain is gone.

Ammonia is tough on every odor from fresh paint to burnt lasagna. Place a small container filled with about 1/2 cup of clear ammonia near an offending smell, being sure to keep the area ventilated, to absorb the nastiness within hours.

Heat the oven to 150 degrees, and set a large pot of water on the stove to boil. Turn off the oven and open the windows to ventilate the kitchen. Place a sturdy container, such as a glass measuring cup or metal bowl, filled with ½ cup ammonia on the oven’s top shelf. Place the pot of boiled water on the bottom shelf. Close the oven and let sit for 8 to 12 hours, then remove the containers of ammonia and water. Open the oven door and air air out for at least an hour before cleaning. Because the grime has basked in ammonia fumes, it should be loosened and easy to remove with a sponge, warm water, and dish soap.

According to recent reports, this method is only recommended for electric ovens, because mixing ammonia with gas can be dangerous. If you choose to use this method on your gas oven, make sure that the pilot light and gas lines are turned off.

According to recent reports, to clean and disinfect kitchen and bath tiles, mix ¼ cup ammonia with 1 gallon of water in a bucket and use a sponge or mop to liberally apply the solution to the tile. Use a soft-bristled brush to scrub any particularly stubborn areas. Finish up by rinsing the surface with clean water and your sponge or mop.

Ammonia’s strong scent can deter unwanted critters. Fill a saucer with clear, unscented ammonia, or saturate a rag or cotton balls with it. Then place in areas that attract pests, such as near garbage cans where raccoons prowl or beside cracks in the basement where mice enter. The smell will remind the varmints of predators, so they’re likely to catch a whiff and turn away, unharmed. That said, make sure to keep the ammonia deterrent out of reach of kids and pets.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Venables and Others: The Dead Pronunciation" (one of A.
  • Sources indicate that although the unfortunate Mr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A conversation with a student reminded me of one of my favorite articles, by my UCLA colleague Henry A. Kelly (who is emeritus in the English Department). It's called "Lawyers' Latin: Loquenda ut Vulgus?," and here's the introduction (though all 14 pages of the article are much worth reading):.

In "Rex v. Venables and Others: The Dead Pronunciation" (one of A. P. Herbert's "Misleading Cases"), Mr. Wick, an advocate making his first appearance in the High Court, tries out his textbook Latin before the Lord Chief Justice. The young advocate, attempting to apply for a writ of certiorari, asks for "a rule of neesee of kairtiorahree." The Lord Chief Justice pretends not to understand this or any other of Mr. Wick's Latin phrases. When ultra vires is rendered ooltrah weerayze, the Court interrupts: "Stop! Listen, Mr. Wick. The two groups of sounds last formed by you have no meaning for me, and I order you not to make use of them again.".

Sources indicate that although the unfortunate Mr. Wick is genuinely baffled by the Court's pronunciation of Latin terms, he is offered scant sympathy:.

Recent findings suggest that it is not for me at my time of life to learn a upcoming language; it is not for the King's judges to remodel their diction according to the whims of pedagogues or the habits of the Junior Bar. The bitter conclusion is, Mr. Wick, that you must go away and learn to pronounce the Latin tongue correctly, according to the immemorial practice of your profession.

Industry observers note that according to the juristic apophthegm, Loquendum ut vulgus, sentiendum ut docti, one should "speak like the common people but understand like the learned." When it comes to legal Latin, lawyers have observed the first part of this advice in various ways. Traditionally, Latin in England and other European countries has not been spoken uniformly but has been pronounced according to the sounds of the vernacular or lingua vulgaris of each region. Nowadays, however, most lawyers must be classed with the vulgus in never having learned Latin, and so they tend to avoid it whenever possible. But when an expression is unavoidable, they give it what they consider to be the "most common" pronunciation, or they imitate the commons in acting according to whim rather than according to rule. The result is what we might charitably call an eclectic or ad hoc approach—we hear, for example, ADD HOCK, ODD HAWK, ADD HOKE, ODD OAK, and so on.

Sources indicate that four different but internally consistent systems of Latin pronunciation have been used in England and America, each entirely "correct" and defensible in theory and in practice. The following analysis is concerned more with showing how the four methods have been adapted to English tongues than with reflecting how each would be spoken by a "native" or purist. My aim, after tracing the vagaries of Latin pronunciation, is to offer some practical recommendations to English-speaking lawyers using Latin phrases….

For the lawyer who occasionally uses Latin words or phrases, I recommend that all  expressions that have survived comfortably from an era when all Latin was pronounced in the English way—for example, et cetera—should continue to be pronounced as English, that is, in the English system of pronouncing Latin outlined above. But when Latin is cited as a foreign language, it should either be pronounced according to the system used by its author (if it is a literary citation) or according to any of the four systems outlined here that seems apt or convenient. Most often, no doubt, the system used will be the one learned in school.

It has been revealed that but lawyers and legal educators should keep in mind the certainty of Herbert's Lord Chief Justice that such "hateful sounds" as "ooltrah weerayze" (for ultra vires) "will never proceed from the lips of an English judge, however many innocent boys are instructed to make them at school." Those who learned the Classical system need to be cautioned against trying to impose it upon all Latin expressions as if it were the only correct, or the most correct, way of pronouncing Latin. To do so would be to mistake the purpose of the scholars who resurrected it. It was intended only for the classics of the Golden Age of Latin, not for later Latin or for technical Latin terms or phrases brought into the various vernaculars in modern times.

According to recent reports, he labels the four methods "Classical (Ciceronian)," "Italian (Dantean)," "Continental (Chaucerian)," and "English (Shakespearean)," and discuss them further. He also cites a medieval source which I quite liked, at least with regard to pronunciation:.

[T]he desire to appear wise among the foolish … is itself a kind of madness.

In a recent development, we considered numerous criteria when narrowing the field of wood stoves to these top selections. According to recent reports, understanding the two types of wood stoves, the materials used to make them, and their heating capacity are all vital when shopping for one of these appliances. Ahead, learn more about these and other important attributes of the best wood stoves.

Sources indicate that wood stoves are available in two types: catalytic and noncatalytic. Catalytic wood stoves differ from noncatalytic in that they produce fewer exhaust fumes and burn more efficiently. In addition to burning wood, catalytic wood stoves also have a combustor that burns smoke and byproducts. This design allows the stove to burn cleaner with a slower burn rate, conserving fuel. Efficiency ratings for a catalytic wood stove range between 63 and 84 percent, making them ideal options for use as a primary source of heat.

In a recent development, noncatalytic stoves are cheaper but not as efficient. They are better suited for use as a supplemental heater.

Industry observers note that most wood stoves are made from one of three materials: cast iron, plate steel, or soapstone. Cast iron, the most commonly used material, heats up swiftly and retains warmth longer than other materials. However, it does crack more easily and is more expensive than other materials.

According to recent reports, plate steel, also a common material used in wood stoves, is durable and retains heat well, though not as well as cast iron. Soapstone is a high-end material for wood stoves. It retains heat better than cast iron, burns cleaner than other materials, and can burn for 24 hours or longer on a single load. Most wood stoves consist of either soapstone or plate steel with a cast-iron door.

A wood stove’s heating capacity determines how large of a space the wood stove can keep warm when it’s running with a full load of wood. The heating area for most stoves ranges from around 1,200 square feet for a small stove to as much as 2,200 square feet (or more) for a large model.

Sources indicate that keep in mind that, unlike a home’s central heating, which distributes heat through ductwork, a wood stove emanates heat from the fire, so the heat isn’t evenly distributed. The farther someone is from the wood stove, the cooler the temperature will be.

The heat output of a wood stove is measured in BTUs (British thermal units). Wood stoves range in BTU output from around 50,000 to 80,000 BTUs. The more BTUs, the greater the size of the space the wood stove can heat. A large 70,000-BTU wood stove can warm up to 2,200 square feet. While BTU level is a great indication of how powerful the stove is, not all manufacturers provide BTU information for their stoves.

It has been revealed that A wood stove’s burn time is the amount of time one load of wood lasts before the stove requires reloading. Each stove’s burn time is determined by how much wood it can hold as well as the heat output of the stove, which can be regulated using the stove’s damper. The firewood type being used also affects burn time. Hardwoods burn more efficiently than softwood, which is less dense and therefore burns more quickly and at lower temperatures.

Sources indicate that wood-burning stoves produce toxic emissions; they create carbon monoxide, which can be deadly if not properly vented outside. Wood stoves are regulated by the Environmental Protection Agency, which performs safety tests on wood stoves to make sure they’re safe for consumer use. The emission limit for wood stoves is 2 grams to 2.5 grams per hour, depending on the type of wood. Catalytic stoves produce well under the EPA’s maximum, with emissions of around 0.5 grams per hour. Never buy a wood stove that is not certified by the EPA.

Perhaps the most important thing to consider when shopping for a wood stove is where it will go in the living space. Most freestanding wood stoves take up a significant chunk of real estate since they measure about 3 feet wide and 2 feet deep and require a buffer around them for safety. Portable models are much smaller—about 20 inches high and 10 inches deep and less than 40 pounds—allowing them to fit in the trunk of a car for a camping trip.

Recent findings suggest that keep in mind that the size of the stove also affects the size of wood they can burn. A standard freestanding or insert wood stove can hold logs up to 18 inches long, whereas portable models can typically handle logs that measure about 8 inches long.

In addition to providing a source of heat, wood stoves also create an ambience that’s similar to a wood-burning fireplace. Most wood stoves have glass windows that allow people sitting around the stove to watch the burning logs.

Some wood stoves also serve as a cooking stove, with flat tops that will support a frying pan or pot. Stoves with cooking functions are typically designed for outdoor use and camping trips.

Recent findings suggest that the best place for a wood stove is as close to the center of the area requiring heat as possible. This allows the stove to radiate warmth in all directions, better heating the space.

Recent findings suggest that hardwoods—which include oak, maple, ash, and birch—are the best-burning woods. They will burn longer and hotter than softwoods like pine and also contain the least amount of pitch and sap inside of them.

Use a brush to sweep up any debris or ash that was not collected by the fireplace’s ash pan. Next, use a wire brush to clean off any buildup inside the flue pipe. Wipe off the exterior of the wood stove with a dry cloth. Be sure to avoid using liquids, which can leave streaks.

The average wood stove should last between 10 and 20 years, depending on usage and care.

Sources indicate that it is safe to leave a wood fireplace on overnight, as long as you follow a few precautions. Allow the wood to burn for a few hours before going to bed. Before turning in for the night, add ash to the burning logs to dampen the flames and slow the burning process. Next, close the stove air vents to reduce the size of the fire, ensuring it will be safe even when burning through the night.

In a recent development, yes. If the indoor wood-burning stove is not properly vented to the outside of the home, it can cause exhaust fumes to collect inside the home, resulting in carbon monoxide poisoning. If a wood-burning stove is installed properly, vented to the outside of the home, and EPA certified, it is safe to use.

String light bulbs are available in a variety of styles and shapes, which can give the strands a unique aesthetic.

According to Friedman, “You’ll also want to look for shatterproof bulbs, ideally LED, since they’re cooler and more efficient.”.

When choosing a bulb size, consider the available outdoor space, ease of installation, and desired look.

Small bulbs are a good pick for small outdoor spaces or garden lighting; they won’t overpower a space or other outdoor decorations. These bulbs are generally more subtle, providing gentle background lighting. They provide less light and are commonly chosen for decorative purposes.

Large bulbs are more striking and offer a bolder look. Their larger size can provide more direct illumination. Generally brighter, they’re well suited to larger spaces that need more lighting. Large decorative bulbs, such as globe bulbs and Edison bulbs, can make a style statement.

Keep in mind that bulb size can affect installation. String lights with small bulbs are generally lightweight and easier to maneuver. They may be easier to install than string lights with larger, heavier, and bulkier bulbs.

Most globe outdoor string light bulbs come in one of three bulb sizes:.

Most Edison-style string light bulbs are an S14 bulb size, which is a medium-size, oval-shaped bulb that’s 32 millimeters (just over 1.25 inches) in diameter.

When it comes to the appearance of outdoor string lights, brightness and color temperature are two of the most vital factors to consider.

Industry observers note that lumens measure the amount of light output from a bulb—the more lumens, the brighter the bulb. When deciding on bulb brightness, take into account the desired lighting effect. String light bulbs can range from 5 to more than 100 lumens per bulb. Customers often choose string lights for their glowy appearance rather than their brightness, so lower lumens often do just fine to set the mood. Lumens are different from wattage, as wattage measures how much power a bulb consumes and not necessarily how bright a light appears.

Lighting color temperature is measured using the Kelvin temperature scale. This scale measures how warm or cool the light appears. Lower numbers on the Kelvin scale look warmer, and higher numbers look cooler.

Most home lighting falls between 2000K and 6000K. Bulbs around 2700K have a cozy, warm white color with a yellow hue, while bulbs over 5000K offer stark, crisp lighting with a blue hue. Warm lighting makes a space look more cozy and inviting, while cool lighting can often appear harsh, especially at night. For this reason, warmer bulbs are generally preferred for ambient outdoor lighting.

Outdoor string lights typically come in lengths of 10, 25, 35, 50, and 100 feet. When choosing the ideal wire length, consider the size of the outdoor space and the lighting layout.

According to recent reports, patio string lights can outline garden borders, wrap around banisters and trees, or suspend over seating spaces. The best way to determine the necessary wire length is to use a piece of twine to measure where the lights will go. If the lights require corded power, make sure to include enough length to reach the outlet, or keep an extension cord handy.

To line one side of an average balcony or small porch, a 10-foot string of outdoor patio lights may do the trick. A small 8-foot-long by 6-foot-wide patio space typically requires 25 to 50 feet of string lighting. A medium 12-foot-square outdoor space may need 50 to 100 feet of string lighting, depending on the desired layout. For more spacious areas or to illuminate a large event, more than 100 feet of string lighting is usually necessary.

Torres v. Carlson, right now pending before the Second Circuit, is a case brought by two Columbia University janitors under the Civil Rights Act of 1871 (KKK Act).

According to their complaint, masked individuals from Columbia University's anti-Israel alliance, armed with hammers, knives, bolt cutters, chains, and zip ties, stormed Columbia's Hamilton Hall and confronted the two men. The janitors' refusal to yield drew the ire of the rioters, who then assaulted them, detained them, and slurred them as Jew-lovers, Jew-workers, and Zionists. The rioters proceeded to seize the building, break windows to chain the doors shut, barricaded themselves inside, and unfurled banners declaring an "Intifada.".

According to recent reports, assuming the allegations are true, this seems like an open and shut case under the KKK Act, which the Supreme Court has described as reaching organized mob violence directed at a protected group and those perceived as standing with it. See Carpenters v. Scott, 463 U.S. 825 (1983).

Industry observers note that nevertheless, the district court granted the defendants' motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim upon which relief could be granted. Covington & Burling has filed an amicus brief on behalf of Jon D. Michael of UCLA Law School, Matthew Segal of Tufts, with the Second Circuit, taking matter with the district court's decisions to:.

(1) resolve at the pleading stage questions of motive in the defendants' favor, crediting the defendants' characterization of their own motives over the plaintiffs' allegations and dismissing explicit antisemitic epithets as irrelevant;.

(2) treat supposed political motive as categorically negating discriminatory animus—disregarding both the mixed-motive framework that operates across federal antidiscrimination law and the settled principle that speech, even on political subjects, can evidence discriminatory intent; and,.

(3) view Jewish disagreement about whether all anti-Zionism is inherently antisemitic as dispositive proof that the specific anti-Zionist rhetoric in this case was not plausibly antisemitic—a standard that conflicts with binding precedent, contradicts how courts apply antidiscrimination law to groups other than Jews, and improperly gives any individual Jew the power to veto discrimination claims by all other Jews.

As an aside, there are several federal court decisions arising out of post-October 7 protest activity that strike many, including me, as applying stricter standards to civil rights plaintiffs claiming anti-Jewish violations of civil rights laws than precedent suggests applies to other plaintiffs.

Sources indicate that though in wintertime a window seat affords postcard-perfect views of snow-covered tree branches, it’s not necessarily the most comfortable perch on a cold day. During the chilly season, so much heat can escape through the panes of glass as well as through any cracks or gaps around the window frame that you’ll want to wrap up in a blanket, or at least put on a sweater, before you risk sitting so close to a window. The Energy Information Administration reports that the average home loses as much as a third of its energy as a result of poor window insulation. Luckily, there are several ways to mitigate this loss. Follow these best practices for how to insulate windows, and you can secure a warmer winter with just one weekend of work.

Bobvila.com may earn a commission from purchases made through these links.

Decades of exposure to the elements can wear away one of your main defenses against heat loss: exterior caulking. Once this begins to crumble, cracks can start to form around the window frame. If your windows are drafty, take swift action to replace the exterior caulking along the window frames before the weather takes a turn for the worse.

Check the weather before you begin the process. For successful application of caulking, you’ll want clear skies for 24 hours—no snow or rain—and, ideally, temperatures above 45 degrees Fahrenheit.

Industry observers note that use a putty knife to scrape window edges clean out the old caulking and peeling paint. Then, wipe the surface clean of any remnants with a damp rag. Let the surface dry for a few hours so the new caulking will readily adhere. It’s best to start the project early in the day to allow enough dry time. You could also leave it to dry overnight.

According to recent reports, load your no-drip caulking gun with a cartridge of silicone exterior caulk and hold it at a 45-degree angle in order to get deep into the cracks around the window frame. Apply a solid, continuous bead of caulking between the frame and the siding, all the way around the window. Any caulk that oozes out of the crack should be pushed in gently with a putty knife.

Allow this to cure overnight to provide the best protection from wind and moisture.

The sash, the part of the window that moves to open and close, is the area most homeowners zero in on when they’re trying to improve window insulation. While this area is important, don’t neglect the glass itself or ignore other draft-curbing solutions. Take a multistep approach to insulating the inside of your windows by employing weatherstripping, window film, and energy-smart window treatments. Though we present this step-by-step approach as a process, you’ll still gain energy savings if you don’t complete every step.

In a recent development, note: When you’re selecting replacement weatherstripping, closely consider the pros and cons of each material. As with many building materials, you get what you pay for in terms of lifespan. Felt, for example, is a common pick for its low price, but it can fail within only a few years. Adhesive-backed foam and tubular gasket stripping, on the other hand, are both cost-effective compression seals that work reliably and provide 3 to 5 years of protection from the cold.

If your weatherstripping is worn or crumbling, it’s time to remove and replace it. Adhesive-backed stripping can simply be pulled up by hand. If the weatherstripping is attached with nails or screws, however, you must first remove the fasteners with a claw hammer or drill before you can lift it away. Once you’ve pulled the weatherstripping off, wipe down the window sash with a damp rag or paper towels and household cleaner. Allow it to dry thoroughly.

Measure your sash carefully, then cut the weatherstripping of your choice to length. Start as close as you can to the end of one side of the sash, peel off any adhesive backing, then carefully press the weatherstripping into place on the sash, making your way carefully to the other end.

“One insulating technique I love and have done many times requires the trim to be off (if, say, you’re installing a newly introduced window or entry door): fill the voids between the door or window jamb and the rough framing with low-expanding foam insulation.”.

—Mark Clement, Contributing Writer.

Industry observers note that with the latest weatherstripping in place, you’ll want to double up your efforts with a window insulation kit. In addition to retaining up to 55 percent of your home’s heat in winter, this type of window covering will reflect heat and block UV rays from passing through uncovered windows, lowering indoor temperatures in summer and saving energy costs year-round. Before you proceed, check to see if your windows are still under warranty; the addition of window film may void the contract. If you’re in the clear, select the best quality insulating window film you can find for the job. Cheap versions can make the outdoors seem darker and even somewhat blurry. While that’s not a big issue for windows in some rooms, for more prominent windows, you may want to invest in higher-quality film that causes little to no loss of clarity and light.

Industry observers note that note: Cheaper methods that produce a similar insulating effect involve heat-and-shrink film or even bubble wrap, but these are often less attractive options that hamper or prevent the use of the windows, or hinder visibility. These inexpensive fixes, however, can be effective, easy to apply, and energy-efficient solutions for basement or attic windows.

According to recent reports, whichever method you choose, installation instructions vary from product to product. In general, start by washing the windowpanes so that no dust or lint gets trapped during application, then follow the manufacturer’s directions for installing the window film.

According to recent reports, best Home blackout curtains keep out up to 99% of light with triple-weave polyester construction and a layer of black yarn. Read the review.

For one last defense against heat loss and drafts, consider hanging thermal curtains. For best insulating effects, install the curtain rod above and past each window on either side so the curtains fully cover the window frame. If it’s not appropriately installed, make adjustments to the rod’s position to maximize heat retention. While other window treatments like blinds or sheers offer some protection from drafts, a set of heavy curtains that you draw shut after dusk can cut heat loss by up to 17 percent.

Sources indicate that whether you ultimately decide to complete just one or all of these steps, you’ll still reap benefits. The more solutions you employ, however, the greater heat retention and energy savings you’ll see, and potentially not just in winter, but all year-round. If you’ve tried all these methods and still have poor window insulation, it might be time to replace your home’s windows.

#79023. No Pseudonymity for Woman Alleging She Was Falsely Accused of Sexual Relationship with Jeffrey Epstein, Doxed

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (797 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

No Pseudonymity for Woman Alleging She Was Falsely Accused of Sexual Relationship with Jeffrey Epstein, Doxed

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (797 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that from Doe v.
  • It has been revealed that jane Doe alleges four X (formerly Twitter) users falsely accused her of having a sexual relationship with Jeffrey Epstein and doxxed her by posting on the social networking site her full name, employment and education history, phone numbers and addresses.
  • [A.] Parties to a lawsuit typically must identify themselves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that from Doe v. Doe (E.D. Pa.), decided today by Judge Gerald Pappert:.

It has been revealed that jane Doe alleges four X (formerly Twitter) users falsely accused her of having a sexual relationship with Jeffrey Epstein and doxxed her by posting on the social networking site her full name, employment and education history, phone numbers and addresses. Doe asserts claims for defamation, false light, public disclosure of private facts and aiding and abetting. She seeks to proceed under a pseudonym because she fears for her safety, along with additional reputational and professional harm. The Court denies the motion because Doe's fear of harm does not outweigh the public's interest in open litigation.

[A.] Parties to a lawsuit typically must identify themselves. Fed. R. Civ. P. 10(a). In "exceptional cases," however, parties may proceed anonymously. To do so, "a plaintiff must show both (1) a fear of severe harm, and (2) that the fear of severe harm is reasonable." Courts balance multiple factors in considering whether to let someone proceed anonymously, including (1) the extent the identity of the litigant has been kept confidential; (2) the bases upon which disclosure is feared or sought to be avoided; (3) the public interest in maintaining the confidentiality of the litigant's identity; (4) whether the problem is purely legal in nature; (5) whether the party seeking to sue anonymously has illegitimate motives; and (6) the universal level of public interest in access to the identities of the litigants. The purpose of this balancing test "is to allow a district court to determine whether a litigant has a reasonable fear of severe harm that outweighs the public's interest in open litigation." ….

The first factor "does not support anonymity where the litigant's identity has never been confidential." Doe has not kept her identity confidential. After Defendants doxxed her, by posting her picture, phone numbers and prior addresses, she publicly responded by "den[ying] the connection to Epstein in the thread of Defendants' posts.".

To establish fear of severe harm, Doe argues that "survivors and other named individuals have reported receiving death threats." Yet she does not allege how she will be threatened if forced to proceed under her real name, and courts reject "claims of harm or generalized fear that are found to be speculative and unsupported by evidence." As she notes, the Defendants have already shared her personal information with the public, so there is no greater risk if she proceeds under her own name.

According to recent reports, doe also alleges a "risk of reputational and professional devastation." But "[c]ourts in this Circuit do not recognize purely social and reputational harms, without more, as valid bases to prevail on this factor." Embarrassment or economic harm is not enough to justify proceeding anonymously either. And because her identity was made public, "litigating publicly will afford Doe the opportunity to clear [her] name" and "will not contribute further to the harm that [she] alleges has already occurred.".

In assessing the public's interest, courts consider whether "other similarly situated litigants [would] be deterred from litigating claims." Doe provides no reason to believe similarly situated litigants would be deterred from bringing defamation claims due to fear of disclosing their identities. The Epstein-related cases she relies upon involve plaintiffs who Epstein sexually assaulted, not individuals falsely accused of having a relationship with him.

Sources indicate that if a plaintiff's claims are purely legal in nature, there is an "atypically weak public interest in knowing the litigant's identity." Doe's claims that Defendants falsely identified her as someone who had a sexual relationship with Epstein are inherently fact sensitive. For example, a key glitch is whether Defendants "knew or were reckless about this falsity and had no good faith basis to claim that Plaintiff was the woman" identified in the Epstein files, and resolving that depends on the nature of the facts known to Defendants.

It has been revealed that there is no evidence that Doe has illegitimate motives to proceed anonymously, which favors anonymity. The universal level of public interest in access to the identities of litigants, however, always weighs in favor of disclosing a plaintiff's identity.

The Court does not diminish the harm Doe claims to have suffered, but she has not established how using her real name would subject her to "severe harm," separate from what she has already allegedly endured from Defendants' past actions. Any harm she may suffer from using her own name is not outweighed by the "thumb on the scale that is the universal interest in favor of open judicial proceedings." ….

Sources indicate that this is consistent, I think, with the cases generally holding that libel plaintiffs can't sue pseudonymously; see Roe v. Smith and the federal cases that it cites.
